messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Ray is a 53-year-old bus driver who lives with his wife in a quiet suburb of a midsized Midwestern city. He came to therapy reluctantly, at his wife’s urging, after months of what he called “just not being myself.” When he finally sat down in the chair across from me, he stared at the floor for a long time before he could speak. What he told me, in fragments, was that eighteen months ago he was raped by a man he had known casually for years—a fellow driver at the depot who had offered him a ride home after a late shift. Ray had been exhausted that night, dead on his feet after a double run, and he accepted. He remembered the man pulling off onto a side road, the click of the door locks, the smell of diesel and sweat. He remembered thinking, *this can’t be happening*, even as it did. He did not report it. He told no one for nearly a year, and when he finally told his wife, he could not look at her.

The memory does not fade. It plays in his mind like a film he cannot turn off, usually at night when he is trying to sleep, but sometimes in the middle of a shift, triggered by something as simple as the sound of a door locking or a passenger’s voice that is too low and too close. When the film starts, the terror comes back whole—the same helpless, animal panic he felt in that car. But what stays with him longer, what he cannot shake for days afterward, is the shame. He feels ashamed of what happened to his body, ashamed that he did not fight harder, ashamed that he had trusted someone. He has come to believe that people cannot be trusted, that there is something fundamentally broken in him for having been fooled, and that whatever faith he once had in the world—in fairness, in safety, in other people—is gone.

The consequences have been slow and corrosive. Ray still drives his bus, because he has to work, but he no longer lets anyone ride in the front seat beside him. He tells himself it is a safety regulation, but he knows it is not. He has become hypervigilant about male passengers who sit too close to the front, especially if they speak to him in a low voice. He has started to feel a knot of dread when he is tired, because he has learned that exhaustion strips away whatever fragile sense of control he has left. On days when he is exhausted, he can feel the memory pressing at the edges of his awareness, and he knows he is more likely to be triggered by a sound—the thud of a door, the hiss of the air brake, the click of a seatbelt—that yanks him back to that side road.

He has also stopped driving with people outside of work. He used to take his wife to dinner, to visit her sister across town, to the hardware store on weekends. Now he makes excuses. He tells her he prefers to walk, or that he is too tired, or that she should take her own car. He knows she is hurt, but he cannot explain it. What would he say? That the passenger seat feels like a trap? That every time someone sits beside him in a moving vehicle, he feels the same helplessness rising? He has withdrawn from his few friendships, stopped going to the union hall, stopped answering calls from the depot. The man who assaulted him transferred to another route, but Ray still sees him sometimes in the break room, and the sight of his face makes Ray’s stomach turn. He has started taking his breaks in the bus rather than in the depot.

What finally brought Ray to my office was a panic attack two weeks ago, in the middle of his route, when a passenger’s bag brushed against his shoulder as she got off. He pulled over, hands shaking, and told the dispatcher he was sick. He drove home in silence and sat in the living room until his wife came home. That night, she told him she was afraid for him, afraid of what he might do to himself, afraid that he was disappearing. He agreed to come see me because he could not bear the look on her face.

He is not sure what he wants from therapy. He is afraid that talking about it will make the film play louder, afraid that I will see the shame in his face, afraid that nothing can change what happened to him. But he is also afraid of losing his wife, of losing his job, of spending the rest of his life locked inside the memory. So he sits in the chair, hands on his knees, and waits to see if I can be trusted.
